rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses asks for eloquent, intelligible speech to communicate revelation effectively; this prayer does not imply that he stammered.
rows.anchor: but to bless him with the power of oratory

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Moses stammered came from the Torah, then entered tafsir and was supported by an invented incident; the Qur’an gives no such indication.
rows.anchor: there are no grounds to believe that he would stammer. This is actually what the Torah says

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah's portrayal of Moses' whitened hand as leprosy illustrates why its claims about a physical defect should not be trusted.
rows.anchor: it regards the whiteness of Moses’ hand to be due to leprosy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A capable speaker may still ask God for fluent expression, especially when explaining religious truths to hostile opponents and hoping to move their hearts.
rows.anchor: Even a very articulate speaker prays and should pray for this ability

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses wanted eloquence to teach and explain religion before people who denied him and threatened his life, not merely to voice slogans or do the task perfunctorily.
rows.anchor: secrets of religion and that too in front of people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an does not support the stammering claim; the Pharaoh's taunt about Moses speaking unclearly is sarcastic, not confirmation.
rows.anchor: cited in verse 52 of S ūrah al-Zukhruf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' prayer sought enough expression for listeners to understand his message and, if possible, for his adversaries' hearts to be won over.
rows.anchor: prowess and expression to make them understand his message

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses asked for Aaron as helper because Aaron could compensate for his limits in oratory; he was an older, trusted brother, reputed for eloquence and good character.
rows.anchor: Aaron (sws) would effectively fill

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Choosing a qualified family member is not nepotism; prayer for divine grace should include righteous family members when their qualities warrant it.
rows.anchor: when the basis of selection is attributes

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Azr means back; strengthening Moses' back means making Aaron his partner so Moses can bear his responsibility properly.
rows.anchor: The request to God by Moses (sws) is to strengthen his back

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses asks for Aaron to share the prophetic mission, with direct divine guidance and protection, rather than merely accompany him.
rows.anchor: to actually ma ke him a prophet as well

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says it is not known whether another prophet was ever made a prophet's helper, citing Maryam 53; God nevertheless accepted Moses' request.
rows.anchor: it is not known if ever a prophet was made the helper of another prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sharing entrusted responsibility reflects true understanding; worldly leaders instead grow jealous of even small positions.
rows.anchor: a true comprehension of entrusted responsibilities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah depicts Aaron as Moses' companion and spokesman and blames him for the Samiri episode, whereas the Qur’an reveals their true character.
rows.anchor: mentioned as a companion and spokesman of Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose of Aaron sharing prophethood was collective glorification and remembrance of God, meaning their public mission as well as private worship.
rows.anchor: individual glorification and remembrance is not implied

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the paired commands, remembrance means warning Pharaoh through the prophetic mission, not only individual devotional acts.
rows.anchor: here remembrance refers to the responsibility of warning the Pharaoh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adjacent glorification and remembrance pair negating what is unworthy of God with affirming His positive attributes; both form faith and character.
rows.anchor: The former is meant to absolve someone of negative traits and the latter affirms positive traits

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Negation precedes affirmation: one must disavow false deities before affirming God alone.
rows.anchor: he cannot be faithful to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses pleads for his request by recalling God's care for him and Aaron, as Zachariah invoked God's prior generosity; divine grace, not deeds, is the best plea.
rows.anchor: basis of His grace and compassion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' plea means that the God who watched over both brothers will not withhold grace as they prepare to advance His cause.
rows.anchor: pleaded to God by referring to His dealing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The matching words for request and plea show that Moses' supplication was granted; the address and answer convey affection and splendour.
rows.anchor: same meaning: request and plea

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God accepted the whole prayer immediately and without exception, including Moses' request for eloquence and Aaron's help; sincere prayer for a right purpose is answered.
rows.anchor: without any hesitation and w ithout any exception

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God recalls saving Moses from Pharaoh's campaign against Israelite boys and arranging for Pharaoh himself to raise him, reassuring Moses not to fear Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: made the Pha raoh bring him up

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words about what was revealed refer to the same divinely planned protection now being disclosed to Moses in detail, beyond what his mother had told him.
rows.anchor: must have become known to him through revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation to Moses' mother was inspiration placed in her heart, which made her certain it came from God.
rows.anchor: instilled it in her heart and she became sure that it was from God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah says Moses' mother hid him for three months and set a cane basket by the bank hoping someone sympathetic would find him; the Qur’an instead says God directed her to place him in the river and promised his return as a messenger.
rows.anchor: God inspired her to put the child in a small trunk

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic account is more logical: without divine direction, Moses' mother could hardly have dared put him into the river.
rows.anchor: account of the Qur ’ ān is more logical

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām in the phrase about the river casting the box is imperative, not the answer to a command; translations treating it as a command-result are mistaken.
rows.anchor: not an answer to a command

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God tells the mother to put Moses in the river, then commands the river to cast him ashore for God's enemy and the child's enemy to find.
rows.anchor: on the one hand, the Almighty sent a revelation to Moses’ mother to put him in a trunk

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's plan made Pharaoh, who claimed divinity and sought to kill Israelite boys, raise Moses and thereby nurture his own eventual downfall.
rows.anchor: the Pharaoh called for his own doom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's bestowed charm made Pharaoh and his wife love Moses; seeing the alone child in the basket stirred their sympathy, especially in Pharaoh's wife.
rows.anchor: And then God Himself cast the reflection of love on him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an says Pharaoh's wife found Moses, correcting the Torah's claim that Pharaoh's daughter and her companions picked him up.
rows.anchor: the Pha raoh and his wife wandered off for a walk

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The suppressed purpose clause means God cast love on Moses so enemies would adore him and he would be raised under God's care; this love guarded and protected him.
rows.anchor: We cast Our reflection of love on you so that even your enemies adore you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the protection “My eyes” refers to God's guarding Moses through the love He placed for him in others.
rows.anchor: by casting His reflection of love on him, God protected Moses (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse compresses much of Moses' story, omitting familiar details and alluding only to selected events before returning to the main discourse.
rows.anchor: Things that did not need a reminder are suppressed here

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brief reference recalls God's promised return of Moses to his mother; al-Qasas supplies the details of Pharaoh's wife adopting him and his sister arranging his mother's nursing.
rows.anchor: the suggestion was accepted and in this manner Moses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Torah's version has Moses' sister ask Pharaoh's daughter for a Hebrew nurse; the Qur’anic account is more logical and natural.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān’s account is more logical as well as natural

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite verb forms suggest Moses' sister approached Pharaoh's wife repeatedly before persuading her to return Moses to his mother; the author presents this as his interpretive translation.
rows.anchor: This makes me repeatedly think Moses’ sister had to go to the Pharaoh’s wife many times

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The killing and Madyan references reassure Moses that the Lord who helped him in past crises will help in future struggles; al-Qasas supplies the omitted context.
rows.anchor: the Lord Who has helped him in such precarious situations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As a mature man, Moses was distressed by Israelite enslavement and abuse; Egyptian authorities feared a capable Israelite leader and may have barred Moses from the city.
rows.anchor: The Israelites w ere slaves in Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses secretly entered the city, aided an Israelite fighting a Copt, and unintentionally killed the Copt with a powerful punch.
rows.anchor: it was such a mighty blow that the Copt died on the spot

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses repented and was forgiven; the next day he rebuked an Israelite for mischief and tried to reconcile two disputants, prompting the Israelite to expose the earlier killing.
rows.anchor: called him a mischievous individual

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After learning that the killing was known and rulers plotted against him, Moses prayed for deliverance and trusted God as he fled to Madyan.
rows.anchor: reposing trust in Him set off for Madyan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At a well, Moses helped two women whose elderly father kept them from pushing into the shepherds' crowd; he watered their flock and prayed for God's provision.
rows.anchor: He got up and made their flocks drink water

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One daughter modestly summoned Moses; their father Shu‘ayb heard his story and reassured him that God had saved him from the unjust.
rows.anchor: God has actually saved him from the unjust

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A daughter recommends hiring Moses, describing him as strong and trustworthy.
rows.anchor: since he was a strong and trustworthy person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shu‘ayb offers a daughter in marriage for eight years' work, with an optional extension to ten, and assures Moses he will find him upright.
rows.anchor: would find him to be an upright person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses accepts the agreement, leaves for Egypt after completing the term, and sees the fire at Mount Ṭūr before being appointed messenger.
rows.anchor: After completing the promised time, Moses (sws) left with his family for Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The longer account from al-Qasas is needed to understand how Ṭāhā's brief allusion to these events works.
rows.anchor: in the absence of this detail, these verses cannot be fully understood

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses had no intent to kill and intervened only to help an oppressed person; the fatal outcome was God's will, but Moses felt accountable and sought forgiveness.
rows.anchor: helping an opp ressed person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses was not acting from tribal prejudice: he later rebuked the same Israelite, and God's forgiveness relieved his grief.
rows.anchor: If Moses (sws) had any prejudice for his people, he would have felt proud

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fear of Pharaoh's unjust rulers added to Moses' sorrow; under a just government he would have presented his case and accepted judgment, but Pharaoh's despotism made that impossible.
rows.anchor: consigning one’s self to the despotic rule of the Pharaoh was tantamount to suicide

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets' errors arise from overreaching in the pursuit of truth, not evil intent; Moses' mistake was virtuous action exceeding its proper limit, which God corrected.
rows.anchor: This mistake of Moses (sws) was in fact an act of virtue

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatannaka means to test, as gold is purified; Moses' repeated hardships prepared him for his mission, from Egypt and Madyan through his later prophetic life.
rows.anchor: The same word is used by the Almighty for trials and tribulations to which Moses (sws) was subjected

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trials train people and polish their best qualities; avoiding a trial from fear of an enemy is like avoiding one's own training, while failure is the real danger.
rows.anchor: qualities found in them are polished further

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hardship tests patience and blessings test gratitude; these virtues ground noble character and lead to a satisfied soul and lasting afterlife bliss.
rows.anchor: In trials of the former type, God wants to inculcate patience in a person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sages differ over whether patience or gratitude is the harder trial; the author judges gratitude harder because few remain grateful after blessings, citing Saba 13.
rows.anchor: the trial of gratitude is tougher

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The higher the rank God intends for someone, the more severe the trials; prophets endured trials beyond ordinary people's capacity.
rows.anchor: the more and the harder will be his trails

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One should fear failing trials and, even more, being spared further trials after repeated failure; such respite to do evil is a severe divine punishment that closes hope.
rows.anchor: what is to be feared even more is that he is relieved of trials

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the verse gives no duration, the al-Qasas account implies Moses stayed in Madyan at least eight and at most ten years as Shu‘ayb's shepherd.
rows.anchor: eight and the maximum must have been ten

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Then you came marks God's plan bringing Moses through successive phases to his appointment; God will again provide opportunities and resources after protecting him from birth.
rows.anchor: whatever happened was according to God’s plan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istana means training someone for a specific objective; Moses' trials trained him for the special task now assigned, which he should undertake in trust of God.
rows.anchor: train someone for a specific objective

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to go is repeated after verses of reassurance: Moses and Aaron are now both sent to Pharaoh because God made Aaron a messenger at Moses' request.
rows.anchor: Aaron (sws) was also included in it because he was also made a messenger at Moses’ request

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Remembering God means prayer and preaching; prayer draws strength from God, the source of true preaching, while a weakened or severed connection drains the mission or turns it into Satan's tool.
rows.anchor: Every task of a prophet constitutes God’s remembrance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Aaron is addressed alongside Moses, this command came after Moses reached Egypt; Aaron was not with him in the valley of Ṭuwā.
rows.anchor: directive was necessarily given later when Moses (sws) had reached Egypt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Soft speech is intrinsic to prophetic preaching and reform, reflecting a teacher's affection and a well-wisher's sympathy, rather than weakness before Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: softness is the nature of every preaching effort

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets do not impose themselves arrogantly; that manner belongs to worldly leaders and underlies contemporary satanic propaganda.
rows.anchor: Imposing one’s self in an arrogant way is the trait of leaders who have become slaves of this world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose of prophetic instruction is to remind people and awaken fear of God; indifferent people may return to guidance when reminded.
rows.anchor: express the purpose of the teaching and preaching of prophets: reminding people and making them fear God
